title: Stridor and the emergency airway
subtitle: Including front-of-neck access and tracheostomy emergencies

sources.title: Multidisciplinary guidelines for the management of tracheostomy and laryngectomy airway emergencies (Anaesthesia 2012)
Difficult Airway Society 2015 guidelines for management of unanticipated difficult intubation in adults
Difficult Airway Society guidelines for awake tracheal intubation (ATI) in adults
Nebulized epinephrine for croup in children

red_flags.text: Stridor at rest, drooling, inability to swallow saliva, or a muffled voice: the upper airway is critically narrowed.
Tripod posture, use of accessory muscles, agitation, or the opposite: exhaustion, quietening and drowsiness. A quieter stridor in a tiring patient is worse, not better.
Falling oxygen saturation is a late sign in upper airway obstruction. Do not wait for it.
A tracheostomy or laryngectomy patient in respiratory distress: assume the tube is blocked or displaced until proven otherwise.
Rapid progression over hours: supraglottitis, angioedema, deep neck infection, or a haematoma after neck surgery.
A bleeding or expanding neck after thyroid or neck surgery with stridor: open the wound at the bedside.

do_now.text: Call for help at once: the most senior anaesthetist and ENT surgeon available. Declare the airway emergency in those words.
Keep the patient upright and calm, with high-flow oxygen. Do not lie them flat, do not send them to the scanner unaccompanied, and do not examine the throat of a child with suspected epiglottitis.
Tracheostomy patient: follow the NTSP algorithm. Apply high-flow oxygen to both the face and the tracheostomy, remove any speaking valve or cap, remove the inner tube, and pass a suction catheter.
If the suction catheter does not pass and the patient is not improving, deflate the cuff. If still not improving, remove the tracheostomy tube.
Waveform capnography on any tracheostomy or airway device as soon as it is available. A flat trace means no ventilation through that route.

assess.text: Phase of stridor: inspiratory suggests a supraglottic or glottic lesion, biphasic a subglottic or upper tracheal lesion, expiratory a lower tracheal or bronchial lesion.
Flexible nasendoscopy by ENT, at the bedside and with the airway team present, if the patient is stable enough. It shows the level and the size of the airway.
In children, score croup severity and look for features that do not fit croup: toxic appearance, drooling, high fever.
Check the bedhead sign for any neck breather: tracheostomy (upper airway present) or laryngectomy (no connection between mouth and lungs). It changes everything that follows.
Track respiratory rate, work of breathing, and an early warning score.

investigate.text: Imaging only once the airway is safe, and only with an escort who can manage it. CT of the neck delineates tumour, abscess and haematoma.
Blood gas when the patient is stable enough; do not distress a child with stridor for a sample.
Blood tests are secondary. No test should delay securing the airway.

resuscitate.text: Croup in children: a single dose of oral corticosteroid (dexamethasone) for all severities, with nebulised adrenaline as a temporising measure in moderate or severe croup.
Nebulised adrenaline buys time but its effect is short-lived. Observe after giving it, and do not discharge on its effect.

Tracheostomy patient after tube removal: oxygenate by the standard upper airway routes with the stoma covered, or via the stoma with a paediatric face mask or laryngeal mask. A laryngectomy patient can only be oxygenated via the stoma.

definitive.text: For an anticipated difficult airway in a patient who is still oxygenating, secure the airway awake, in theatre, with a surgeon scrubbed and the neck marked for front-of-neck access before anything else is done.
Cannot intubate, cannot oxygenate: proceed to emergency front-of-neck access through the cricothyroid membrane using the scalpel, bougie and tube technique, as DAS describes.

Tracheostomy patient with an upper airway who cannot be oxygenated after tube removal: secondary oxygenation by oral intubation, or by intubating the stoma with a small tube, preferably guided by a fibreoptic scope.
Treat the cause once the airway is secure: drainage of an abscess or haematoma, treatment of angioedema, or a planned surgical tracheostomy for an obstructing tumour.

escalate.text: Senior anaesthetist and senior ENT surgeon for every stridulous adult. Paediatric anaesthesia and paediatric ENT for a child.
Critical care for every patient whose airway has been at risk, including those who improved with adrenaline or steroids.
Do not transfer a patient with a threatened airway to another hospital without first securing the airway or having airway-competent staff in the vehicle.

notes: The question in stridor is not 'what is the diagnosis' but 'how much time is there'. Bring the people who can secure the airway before you need them.
Every tracheostomy and laryngectomy patient should have a bedhead sign. The single most important fact on it is whether the patient can be oxygenated from the mouth.
Front-of-neck access is a decision, not a skill problem. The failure in most reported cases is the delay in declaring 'cannot intubate, cannot oxygenate'.
